In the “floating world” of the Edo period (the Tokugawa shogunate, 1603 CE – 1868 CE) of Japan, in the taverns and gathering places where samurai spent time after a day of bureaucratic administration, they told stories of other samurai: armored warriors sweeping across a field of battle, daring escapes, cunning ninja, and heroic leaders. These were the stories that shaped our impression of feudal Japan; these were the stories of the Sengoku Jidai, the time of war.

The Sengoku period, beginning in the late 15th century CE and ending near the start of the 17th, was a time, too, of countless possibilities for Japan’s future. Even as feudal clans struggled for control over the imperial palace, Christianity began to make inroads in the south, gunpowder took to the field, lordless peasant republics flickered in and out of existence. At its end, the chaos was put to rest with the ascendance of a powerful shogunate, the establishment of the prosperous Edo period…and the closing of Japan to the world.

“Sengoku” means “the time of the country at war,” and as such does not correspond with any of the traditional divisions of Japanese history, which are normally named for the dynasty in the imperial palace at the time. Formally, most of Sengoku was during the Muromachi or Ashikaga period (1336 CE – 1573 CE), named for the shogunate ruling at the time, though the first part of this era did not devolve into the chaos – that which we call “Sengoku” marks a period of instability out of which the legends of feudal Japan were born.

Governance at this time was nominally done by the Emperor, but in reality he had little impact upon the practical considerations of rule. That in turn was conducted by the shogun, the military leader, appointed from among the group of daimyo, local rulers. Clans vied for this position, though for years the shogunate was dominated by only a few.

Dating the actual start of the Sengoku period is difficult, as the signs of decline within the Ashikaga shogunate had been showing for some time – wars in the Kanto region (eastern Japan, including what would later be Tokyo), increasing power of local daimyo, and unrest against the shogun. But if we want to pin the wars to an exact event, one could do worse than to point to the Onin War, which devolved into a massive street battle that began with a contested claim between two rival clans and ended with the widespread destruction of Kyoto.

In its wake, the Onin War solidified not only the idea that the emperor existed at the whim of the shogun, but also that war was a means to solidifying power. This held true for powerful clans as much as peasants, for would-be warlords as well as monks. Many sought new potential in the chaos, some of whom were local daimyo, but including configurations not seen before in Japanese history – a group of peasants animated by the populist Pure Land Buddhism organized into the Ikko-Ikki; the daimyo Otomo Sorin leveraged Christianity and foreign connection as a means towards a new order.

In this age when everything seemed possible through battle, numbers as well as technology were the key to victory. Armies were no longer hundreds of warriors; they were tens of thousands. Logistics became increasingly important as armies went to fight in places far afield from their home ground, and in later periods, weapons such as firearms entered the fray. The nobility constructed castles and fielded heavily-armored samurai for defense, while the commoners organized into so (communities) or ikki (larger leagues). As foreign goods flooded in (and as daimyo competed for status in the throne room as well as on the battlefield), cities and communities of artisans grew.

One warlord above all emerged out of this chaos – Oda Nobunaga. The Nagoya-based warrior seized Heian-kyo (Kyoto) in 1568, putting an end to the war of all against all…and beginning the war of Oda against all who resisted. Oda’s reign was both brutal towards opposition and permissive towards trade. But when one of his vassals turned on him, trapping him deep within his own territory with his warriors far afield, Oda committed suicide rather than face defeat.

The next of the great warlords of this era was Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a retainer of Oda who avenged Oda’s betrayal and continued his campaign of unification. But Toyotomi sought to go further, seeking to conquer not only Japan, but Ming China by way of Korea. His two invasions were stopped, and upon Toyotomi’s death, his most powerful subordinate, the lord of Edo, Tokugawa Ieyasu, sought the perilous seat as the lord of Japan, defying the claim of Toyotomi’s heir.

He faced off against Toyotomi clan loyalists at the Battle of Sekigahara, a fight involving around two hundred thousand warriors and, on Tokugawa’s side, a secret stash of firearms. The slightly outnumbered Tokugawa emerged the victor, sending the Toyotomi clan into chaos. The victorious Tokugawa was appointed shogun by the emperor and so ushered in the Edo period.

But Sengoku was not all war and chaos. The consolidation of lesser daimyo into greater ones, especially towards the end of Sengoku and the rise of Edo, formed some of the key moments that moved Japan towards a modern nation-state. Here was a separation of classes, a system of taxation (the Edo-era kokudaka), a notion of the public (kogi) separate from the bakufu (feudal system). The bones of a middle class of artisans, the transformation of samurai from battlefield heroes to bureaucratic administrators, all occurred within this transition. And a recognition arose of the dangers of outside interference – whether from foreign religion or gunpowder.

Edo was, in contrast, a time of isolation and prosperity, a long period of calm following the chaos of the Sengoku period. It was a time when the stories of battles and ninja, ghosts and treachery of that time turned from history into legend, and it is through that lens that the romance of the time becomes refracted.

Built in 1333 during the war that ended the Kamakura shogunate and ushered in the Muromachi period, Himeji Castle was extensively expanded in 1581 by Toyotomi Hideyoshi during his reign. It occupies the center of the city of Himeji and is the largest castle in Japan. Key in its style is Toyotomi’s large central keep, but despite its more palace-like appearance in comparison to European castles of the time, Himeji is built for defense. It is riddled with points where archers or gunners could attack invaders from relative protection, a deliberately obtuse approach in which invaders could get lost, and extensive storerooms from which defenders could draw during a siege.

But it never fell victim to such a fate. Instead, Himeji became a cultural touchstone for Japanese culture from the Edo period onward. From its association with Toyotomi to the ghost in its courtyard (made famous by the illustrator Hokusai), the “White Egret Castle” has become a symbol of feudal Japan.

Sengoku was a time of flux. War and the changing order of power were constants. It is little wonder, then, that the notions of simplicity and peace emphasized by Zen Buddhism became attractive. Tea houses – chashitsu – were places where this simplicity was matched with an emphasis on rural peace, on natural settings and simplistic aesthetics. These spaces were focused around the aesthetic of beautiful decay (wabi-sabi) and the imperfections and decline of everyday life. They were places for the upper classes (such as they were in Sengoku), both islands of tranquility and settings that could be both beautiful and inexpensive, at least in terms of materials. Toyotomi Hideyoshi himself was an avid patron of tea houses – though, of course, his was made of gold.

The Sengoku period was a time of mass conflict where clans vied for power. That the Emperor held the supreme title was not in doubt, but real control rested with the shogun – a military ruler who made the key decisions in the empire. The conflict shattered the country, a war of (nearly) all against all, and into this fray came Oda Nobunaga, the first of the “unifiers” of the period. Oda was never shogun, but instead is called “tenka bito,” the “Ruler of All under Heaven” as a sign of his immense political power. However, appropriate to the time, he was betrayed and killed by a disloyal vassal, and the mantle of tenka bito would move to Oda’s avenger, Toyotomi Hideyoshi.

In the chaos of Sengoku, it was not only the clans who vied for power and influence. Associations of commoners or samurai that came together with a clear goal in mind enabled the growth of what might in later years be called civil society. Most famous of these were the Ikko-Ikki, religious peasant associations that marshalled armies and challenged the clans themselves.

Guilds were a powerful force in early medieval Japan, a force that came into conflict with clan leaders who wanted this power for themselves. A policy of free markets and open guilds – rakuichi-rakuza – was a means to this end, allowing for a profusion of merchants, especially in castle towns. Although it brought prosperity, it centered much of this wealth with daimyo (local rulers), and at the same time, the numbers of new merchants meant smuggling rings and corruption became more commonplace.

If the Sengoku period was a great fire, the Kinsei – the Golden Age – was the steel that emerged from it. The new Tokugawa shogunate that followed the Sengoku period had new Sengoku-forged political structures that were more modern than the feudal systems that preceded it, new systems of taxation, and increased bureaucratic control. Samurai went from mastering the katana to wielding the writing brush – and the state thrived.

To get at the “real” history of the shinobi (or ninja), we have to look at the peasant rebellions of the Sengoku era – the Ikko-Ikki and others. In the chaos of conflict, powerful non-noble families had to fend for themselves. Without the honor of aristocracy to uphold, non-nobles had a fair bit of leeway to use unconventional methods: impersonation, sabotage, infiltration, and the like. While the popular-culture image of a shinobi is of a masked assassin, most shinobi were not slinking around in black throwing shuriken at people – rather, they performed tasks such as posing as commoners or farmers to infiltrate a besieged fortress, or acting as enforcers or guards.

In this way, a lot of ninja tools and implements look like farmer’s tools – the kama (sickle), for instance, rather than the sword. The iconic shuriken, of course, existed, and came in a number of uses and variations, from setting fires to planting caltrops to short-range thrown weapons. Of all of the clans of shinobi, it is the Iga, and the ninja retainer to Tokugawa, Hattori Hanzo, who has been best-remembered.

The samurai is the iconic symbol of the Sengoku period, both for us now as well as for the Japanese storytellers of the Edo period. Their reality was a little different. The term changed its meaning over time, from a noble knight before Sengoku, to a much broader definition during Sengoku, to a sort of scholar-bureaucrat during Edo. In Sengoku, a samurai was a person who attended to a daimyo, a lord. This could mean a wide variation in class and background, though in that time samurai were always those who served with arms, and were distinguished from the common ashigaru, the infantry. Samurai, for instance, could hold last names, and skill at battle could elevate someone to the samurai rank – and a skilled samurai could be elevated to a Sengoku daimyo.

While samurai are most often thought of in association with the katana, the Japanese sword that marked a lighter and faster weapon than the earlier tachi, they could wield a variety of weapons and fought on horseback as well as on foot. Female samurai (onna-musha, technically of the warrior, or bushi, class) often preferred the naginata, the glaive.

Eighteen times I have escaped from ten thousand deaths.
"Fifty years of a human's life – these are but a dream, an illusion."
"They look strong; they are weak. Their power only comes from your submission."
"People are castles. People are walls. People are moats."
"On all the islands, glittering lights appear, in the spring sea."

In Sengoku Japan, power belongs to the bold. In the chaos of conflict, the lowliest ashigaru can rise to the title of samurai, and a minor lord can dream of becoming shogun – provided one survives the storm. The time has come to make a name for yourself.

When planning your Buildings, remember that Culture and Science Buildings do not have their normal adjacencies with Sengoku. They do still benefit from Wonder adjacency, but you should save the good terrain spots for other Building types!
As Sengoku Japan, complete 4 Diplomatic or Militaristic Major Triumphs in a single Apex Age.
As Sengoku Japan, complete the Himeji Castle.
Contains a new Exploration Age Civilization, Sengoku.

Armed monks patrol the town, having lost faith in the governance of their lord. The modesty of their robes clashes with the iron binding their staves – but at least here, the peasants have protectors.
Lend them support, and take a cut of offerings.
Undermine them with a few scandals.

The hyakushodai of a number of villages bring a host of concerns to their lords: taxes are too high, and guards are too quick to raise their weapons. But all this could be forgiven, they say, with a grand show of support at the upcoming Gion Matsuri.
The lords' parade floats will be the most beautiful, and the most expensive.
There is plenty of room in the dungeons for whiners.
{1_reward}, but 1 Improvement is Pillaged in each Unhappy Settlement.

Blocking the way into the temple of {1_religion}, a group of zealots accosts anyone who will stop and listen to them. Their faces are familiar, but the garb they wear is foreign, as are the tomes they brandish, and the ideas they preach.
The spirits of the land speak for themselves.

A samurai picks up an unfamiliar weapon from the battlefield, running a hand over its firing mechanisms. Ignoring the smell of sulphur and blood, he pays respect to the dead soldier who once wielded the tool.
This enemy must not be underestimated.
Turn the enemy's own tool against them.

There are no winners in war, only opportunists. This is what the commander repeats to herself as advisors settle into the honmaru. As they bicker prematurely about the ensuing war's spoils, the commander slides the fusuma shut.

Fresh from the battlefield, a samurai kneels to receive his lord's praise. Bringing his forehead to the ground, he pauses longer than is customary and returns to an upright position. The lord is surprised when the samurai's gaze does not meet his own.
Who knew commoners could rise to such greatness!
When did the samurai start allowing commonborns?
As distant wars rage, a young woman retreats into the chashitsu for solace. She kneels on a tatami mat and unpacks the simple chabana – her hands shakes as she lays out utensils to make tea.
These simple aesthetics help calm the spirit.
Beautiful scenery would make a better distraction.

Hoping to convince visiting nobles of the benefits of Himeji castle’s unique layout, Toyotomi Hideyoshi sends a servant to guide them through the deceptively tall castle. What started as a tactical demonstration turns into concern as the group has yet to reemerge.

Under nightfall, a shinobi watches as guards patrol their lord's personal chashitsu. Quick and quiet, he squeezes through the nijiriguchi and scans the room for his target, only to meet the gaze of a stunned handmaiden holding a tray of tea.
He was just inspecting the latest blend.
The Good Doctor and the Samurai

As the veteran samurai takes him on a tour of his estate, Dr. Rizal takes note of both a tranquil rock garden and a training dojo. His host replies that discipline is not innate, but cultivated and honed.

A traveler boards her train home and sits by the window, fiddling with an amulet she bought at the jinja. She muses on what stood out most during her trip as her view shifts from metropolitan grays to rural greens.

The daimyo of Hojo Railways and the Transportation Ikki are fighting, again. A shinobi was caught planting demolition charges at TI’s power station, and confessed to being in Hojo’s employ. TI, in a surprising turn of events, decided to make the saboteur public, rather than simply hiring their own shinobi in order to get revenge.
Strength. The Ikki does not need to stoop to sabotage.
Weakness. Hojo will strike better, next time.

Bushido. Honor. The code of the samurai and way of the warrior. These mean much to the poets and artists of Japan. For the warriors and rulers of Sengoku, however, these are a veneer placed upon the boldness with which power is seized, and the tenacity with which it is held.
But the legend is what matters. Ensure that the legend is what survives, not the messiness of conquest.
Strive for openness in all things. Even if it makes for a less compelling story.

Hold a tea ceremony for the master. One last time.
The cherry blossoms descend. The tea is sipped, the bowls shattered. Sen no Rikyu composes a poem to the dagger that will take his life.
